description: Busco personas creativas y comprometidas, con habilidades en programación, análisis de datos, diseño o ciencias, que quieran resolver desafíos reales y crear soluciones innovadoras para NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Don Rover's Workshop is a multiplayer learning platform that turns a classroom into a Mars colony that must survive. Each crew of four students takes one specialty: Power, Life Support, Astrobiology or Habitat. IX, the colony's AI, builds every mission from real NASA data: recent space weather from DONKI and scientific studies from NTRS and OSDR. Each specialty holds a piece of information the others lack, so the crew can only find the best decision by cooperating. Their choices change a persistent 3D Mars colony that is saved from one class to the next.

It runs as a PWA in the browser. The teacher's projector is the host, and students join from their phones by scanning a QR code, with no accounts needed. The game keeps working if the AI or servers are unavailable.

It addresses the challenge by making real NASA science hands-on and understandable for ages 7-15: students use space weather and space science studies to make concrete survival decisions, building teamwork and critical thinking. It matters because it brings NASA data into the classroom, in Spanish, making space science engaging and accessible for young learners.
details: WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS Don Rover's Workshop (https://tallerdedonrover.vercel.app) turns a classroom into a Mars colony that has to survive. A crew of four students each takes one specialty (Power, Life Support, Astrobiology, Habitat), linked like the systems of a real base. IX, the colony's AI, generates each mission from real NASA data: recent space weather from DONKI and scientific studies from NTRS and OSDR. Claude chooses the mission and writes each specialty's task, while a deterministic game engine calculates all scores and consequences. A mission runs through briefing, discovery, crew challenge, a global emergency with specialty minigames, results and debrief. There are six missions and three difficulty levels (ages 7-9, 10-12, 12-15), in a 40-minute class pace or a 10-minute demo pace. The teacher's browser (the projector) is the host, and students join from their phones by scanning a QR code over WebRTC. No accounts are needed. BENEFITS Students practice teamwork, communication and critical thinking while applying real NASA science to concrete decisions. The teacher gets a console with hints, pause, extra time, practice bots, a mission log and a CSV report. Names and logs are moderated. The game still works if the AI, database or NASA services are unavailable. INTENDED IMPACT We want more kids to meet real NASA data and space science in a fun, collaborative way in their own language (Mexican Spanish). The colony is saved from class to class, so progress carries over and gives students a reason to come back. TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY TypeScript, React 19, Three.js, GLSL shaders, CSS, SQL (PostgreSQL), Vite, PeerJS (WebRTC) with Supabase Realtime as a fallback, Supabase Postgres, Vercel serverless functions, the Anthropic Claude API, the NASA DONKI, NTRS and OSDR APIs, and Web Audio. It is a PWA. The only hardware needed is a projector and students' phones. CREATIVITY Every specialty holds a piece of information the others lack, so students must cooperate. Numbers are seeded per crew, so copying another team does not work. The 3D Mars world is fully procedural, with Mars gravity (3.72 m/s2), and it changes with the crew's decisions. Minigames replace button-tapping with realistic tasks that show real NASA data. IX adapts: it sends hints when a class struggles and opens bonus emergencies when it is easy. The emergency gets harder if the Sun is actually active. FACTORS WE CONSIDERED Different ages and difficulty levels; school networks that block direct connections (automatic relay fallback); low-end phones (adaptive 3D quality); student privacy (no accounts, no personal data); safe AI use (structured, validated outputs, and the AI never decides scores); and scientific honesty (colony percentages and radiation doses are simplified game values, and the Unknown Signal is fiction).
